Having had some life threatening medical issues (and also not being able to work due to them) a few times; as well as having to run a business and actually seeing the numbers most people dont actually see; I've learned a few harsh lessons.

1) Health Insurance is like Car insurance: If the 1 in a million chance happens, and you get into a horrible accident that would cost you $1M to fix; the Insurance pays for it. But the only way it works, if if 1 million people each pay $1+, so that the 1 in a million chance is covered. Basicly Insurance is the Lottery, where you only "win" if Big, Rare, Bad Thing happens.

2) Health Care is like Auto Maintance. It's fundementally a 100% chance that it has to happen, so there is no way to "insure" against it. It's simply a cost of existance.

And this is where one finds out (especially as an employer) that health maintance (insurance + rountine care) is realy really expensive. As in the "you have no idea how mind numbingly, outragously, Louis-the-Leg-Breaker Mob Loan Shark charges less of a rate increase every year" kind of expensive.

I often wish we had a hybrid system; where taxes pay for the main health care enviroment; but if you want a higher (or faster) level of service, you have the option to buy "private" insurance or care or whathave you. The only issue with this system is the "rationing" that must occur due to no resourse being unlimited. But just as to my experiences, most of the "rationing" I've seen in other countries is simply the wait times for optional / non-time-critical services.

3) Going Bankrupt while HAVING health insurance: Big life lesson here with that number (ouch!).... ~HEALTH~ insurance dosn't pay the rent. Or electricity bill, or food, or the cat's dinner. So when you can't work for a long period; the health insurance may be paying the doctors; but it's not paying the rent. And....... bingo..... another statistic to the "bankrupt WITH health insurance" number.

So other then comiserating, my one peice of advice: Seriously. Get a Short Term / Long Term disability policy. 'cause even with health insurance, you also need ~~income~~ insurance. Some of those policies also cover pregnancy, so if you are a two-income household; and you have another child; you don't lose all of that 2nd income for the time.

I would make a fishing simulator. However, this game would require you to buy several peripherals. Let me explain:

I love fishing for large fish, especially in saltwater. However, due to work/living 3.5 hours from the coast, I only get to go once or twice a year. In the theme of Rocksmith, where you plug your guitar in to your console of choice/PC, I would like to design a pulley/winch device that you connect the line of your existing fishing gear to, which will simulate the effect of the fish trying to escape after being hooked. Combined with the incoming wave of VR head sets, I think this could be an incredible experience for people who love angling as much as I do, but don't have the time/ability to spend $2000 for a 6 hour trip chasing marlin, sailfish, and tuna several times a year.

Of course, it would be expensive(buying the tackle if you don't have it already, the winch system), as well as potentially dangerous for the gamer (line breaks, getting digits wrapped in the line), but that's how it is in real life. There are also limitations, such as not being able to cast if you are fishing with artificial lures for freshwater species such as large mouth bass, so the game would mainly be based on trolling/live baiting for large fish, which is fine with me, but perhaps not the majority of fisherman. It would probably also be limited to PC, which is fine with me, but perhaps not to everyone.

All in all, I think it would be a fun game though.

I was inspired by the implied history in Shadow of the Colossus and came up with a psuedo city-building RPG game, where you played as a guardian that had to protect your worshipers from plagues, disasters, armies, and other massive guardians/titans/monsters. Rather than a top-down traditional city-builder, your worshipers would attract followers and build temples to enhance your powers based on how you address certain challenges.

For example: if you took direct action, you would get personal bonuses that made you more badass and capable for future challenges. If you took a passive route and gave your people the opportunity to solve their own problems, you would get skills that buff and support your people. Avoiding problems give you stealth boosts, engineering solutions give you trap/world building powers, peaceful actions gave you social/diplomacy abilities that would work on even natural events (e.g. even the gods are swayed by your words.)

Overall, I'd like the game to be an at-your-own-pace sandbox (Terraria, Dwarf Fortress), with the wish fulfillment of an RPG (Morrowind, Mass Effect), and the consequences of a social game (Walking Dead? Never played). I would like every skillset to be applicable to every problem. Some may be more effective than others, but there should not be a "best" or "broken" way to play, or an "underpowered" skill choice.

Of special note is the diplomacy option stated earlier. Too many games treat dialogue and combat as separate aspects, and that doesn't feel right. I'm the dragonborn, head of every guild, and richer than my wildest dreams; they should NOT want to fight me. If my character is a city-dwelling craftsman, I should be able to trade goods and coins for safe passage. If I am famous for being the defeater of a great evil, they should fear me. A clever rogue might be able to befriend them. This is MUCH more freedom than choosing between kill with bow, kill with sword, kill with magic.
Yeah, but I'm not a fan of most top-down games like that. I wanted the game to play like an RPG, where your people were a constantly adapting companion.

My inspiration came mostly from Planescape: Torment, easily having the best storyline of anything I've ever experienced.

Had this idea for an MMO that used separate planes to connect to other worlds, and had gates to connect these worlds. You could have your own plane of existence (to build a home or a guild) that could change in size, but there was also static planes that were part of the main storyline. The world constantly grew (since it would be incredibly easy to add another plane with another gate that takes up no space), and forced you to explore. You became weaker as you travel further and further away from your home dimension, which forces you to become stronger if you want to explore. Fighting in a region slowly teaches you different combat functions (like using health for abilities), and the monsters in said region are best defeated with the skills you learn from there (like monsters doing bonus damage based off of your missing magic). In a sense, the game is about adapting to every situation, until you are attuned to the universe.

I'd make an FPS focused on 1v1 combat where you select characters like you would a fighting game, or Dota. Each character would spawn with a unique set of weapons including a grenade, side arm(pistol sized weapon), and rifle or launcher (shotgun/assault rifle/sniper rifle/rocket launcher/etc...). Characters would also have a variety of movement characteristics. This would include circle/strafe jumping, dodge jumping, dash jumping, triangle jumping, blinking, etc...

Additionally with this being a futuristic shooter for lore and gameplay reasons players would not have health or armor. In this reality every gun is so powerful that it would obliterate anything in one shot. Instead characters are equipped with a non-replenishable energy shield. Basically you only have one life bar and there is no way to replenish it. I think dueling FPS games have a bit of a problem with players not dieing and it being too easy to hold control of the map for the whole match. This paradigm enables character artists more freedom to design cool looking characters while resolving the issue of overly dominate map control.

However players still need something to control and give them an advantage to make the game more interesting than just placing your cursor over someone's head.

In place of health or armor pickups would be "EX" pickups. Players would earn EX meter either by hitting their targets, or picking up vials/kegs around the arena. Additionally meter would persist through death. You use your meter either by pressing a specific EX button while shooting (for newbies) or by pressing the key to swap to that weapon and the fire button at the same time. Each gun has it's own EX shot and can vary in many different ways. Larger projectile, faster projectile, more damaging, larger knock back, forces popup, etc. In addition using EX removes all weapon swap times so players can really dish out the pain when they have earned meter.

Players will also be able to pick up and control various super and ultra weapons. Super weapons would spawn about as frequently as normal weapons in typical arena shooters and do marginally more damage, but ultra weapons would spawn at about the frequency of red armor or mega health and deal massive damage. Ultra weapons may also be universally damaging powerups like for instance a radiation pickup where your opponent is damaged over time, but not you.

Again, the idea is to give players tools to kill one another, not keep themselves alive.

Hate to add to a pile here, but I'd create the "ideal" MMO. (At least in my eyes)

  • Quests are actually interesting and rewarding, not treated as just a means of leveling up
  • Lore is deep yet easy to learn about
  • World is almost completely dynamic, pretty much anything is possible
  • Players have influence on the world, and your adventures have more of a personal feeling to them rather than having that "just another player" feel
  • World events are actually important, and can give a different face to the world around the player
  • NPCs have impressive AI, aren't just quest givers and impact the world like players do but in a smaller way
  • Combat isn't braindead button mashing and actually takes skill to take down your opponent, whether AI or an enemy player
  • Playing with others is important, but not totally necessary for those wanting to be a "lone wolf"
  • Guilds are important and influential

This is just from my imagination, though. I don't know how many resources or how much money it would take to actually create something like this, nor if it's actually that plausible.

3 planets, 3 factions. FPS/3rd person perspective on a massive scale.

Faction 1- gamers Side A, planet 1 Faction 2 - gamers Side B, planet 2 Faction 3 - gamers Side C, planet 3 You could have a wildcard faction of devs.

Each planet is roughly the size of a planetside 2 planet. However, you need to build an entire infrastructure. So while you have people who loved playing SWG and being a doctor, you could be a doctor and treat war-wounded. You could be in trade and deal parts and pieces with other members of your faction.. such as wood to the home builders and they trade you back ore they mined. Naval research and scout the lands for plans/kill enemies for plans. Capture ships and reverse engineer them. Be a regular infantry player and belong to a fighting family and push for territory gains on other planets. Of course you'll need the space pilots to get you to and from the planets.. who will need the space fighters to escort.. and bombers to clear the land once you've made it through space to your planet destination.

You want income to help build better outposts on your land? Mine ore, have your engineers build something, reinforce with weapons and people.

Tim logs in at 8pm.. he's part of a crew that watches Area XYZ for a few hours. Maybe he specializes in ground to air weapons. Tim owns an apartment, Bill is a builder in town and he's not an FPS gamer, but Bill loves playing the Sims so he finds his niche in building homes for gamers. Tim escorts Bills family in resource gathering on their planet..in turn, Bill builds a great house for Tim's family. Chuck belongs to the other faction and knows that resources gathered on a different factions planet are given at +100% rate.. so he's flying some space monkeys in to mine Tim's planet. A battle is waged. It's survival for each faction. You cannot live on your own land and must consume the other planets in order to thrive. Also, there is an end point to the game.. and it resets. A winner needs to be chosen.

Every type of gamer can find something they enjoy doing within this game. Love and RTS and building a perfect base defense? Be on the defensive engineering team! Are you a badass old school FPS gamer and you want to get up in someone's grill? Go infantry. Like racing games? Pick up a nice dune buggy and shuttle people through bad lands.

You would need your economy to thrive in order to have a successful faction.

Actually got a concept at hand, but you should always keep in mind that the industry barely has any need for "idea people" - most coders, environmental artists and whathaveyou have more ideas of their own than they could realistically ever turn into games. Still, here goes:

"The Hunt" is a first-person horror adventure, set in a large derelict industrial structure. The players controls a young woman that has been given the 'role' and name of the Hare, and must now make her way through the complex. As she ventures through the ruins, Hare meets various other humans wearing animal masks – those wearing the masks of predatory animals will be hostile to hare and will her attack her in a fashion consistent with their respective masks, while those wearing the masks of herbivores may ignore her, help her, or flee from her. The player may choose to either remain in Hare's role (permanently running away from predators), or may try to break out of the role (defending herself from predators and potentially even killing them). Both options come with their own sets of consequences - killing predators allows Hare to loot parts of their costumes which serve as uprades and unlock new abilities, but will also make the game harder and may make herbivores hostile to her.

It's the farming game I've always wanted that no one will ever make.

I've always wanted the perfect zombie game. You start off in your house, that date that time. You turn on the TV. Just some news about a virus or something. You make some toast, and while eating it you hear "This is a confirmed zombie virus." You stare at the screen for a minute, and then notice a figure behind the newscaster. It lunges at them, knocking them down to the ground and knocking the camera over, to a front seat of the person being devoured, until a splash of blood hits the lense and covers it. You stare at the screen, until you hear a banging at your door. Just in case, you grab your Glock, and cock it. Then you open your door. A zed stands there, in a tattered suit. You run back, and aim. The bullet sends the zombie's brains through the air and onto your floor. You stare at the body for a minute, before moving it out of the way and cleaning up the blood, skull fragments and brain on your floor. You close your door, lock it, and then check your kitchen. You have enough food for a couple days, and the water's still running. You log onto your computer, and watch some funny cat videos, in an attempt to calm down. Then, you hear banging at your back door, and realize you hadn't locked it. The door soon gives way, and a few zombies stumble into your room, and you remember you left your Glock downstairs. You get bitten, and then torn apart, screaming all the while.

LIMBO - $4.99 : Play Store link - Link to free demo

LIMBO is an indie horror-platform game where you start with no knowledge of what is going on and slowly unravel the plot while trying to stay alive

For me, there will never be a game that comes close to this; I don't get scared playing games and very rarely do I jump due to being frightened, but this game does both of those things to me. Not only is the atmosphere near perfect, but the controls are easy and responsive, the plot is compelling and mysterious, and the sounds/music bring every interaction to a whole new level. I'm not a big gamer on my phone, but this is one that I highly recommend if you're looking for a fantastic game and sucks you in.

Music Mate - US$3.99 (Free to Install, InApp Purchase to unlock) : Play Store Link

"This app is for use with the Google Play Music™ app and service. You must have the Google Play Music app installed and setup for this app to work properly. Make sure you have the latest version too.

This app will allow you to download your music directly from the cloud and import it into your local device library so you can play it in ANY media player installed on your device."

This app does what it says on the box. It will download the music from your Google Play Music cloud storage to your local device storage retaining tags and album/artist name, so you can actually use a decent music player. The app is free to install and you can download up to 50 tracks to test it out. If you want to download more you need to buy the unlock key via InApp Purchase.

Note: This app was formerly known as "Cloud Music Importer".

Journey - Free w/~$4.50 premium : Play Store Link

Journey is a journaling app that will look familiar to anyone that's heard of Day One on iOS/Mac, except it's for Android/Chrome so it's available for a lot more people. Great for anyone that wants to start journaling or keeping a diary but doesn't want to post it all on a private/public tumblr or blog. The dev really takes the journaling experience seriously with great design, different views, automatic tagging of location and weather, cross-posting to Facebook/Twitter/Tumblr, and Google Drive backup and sync.

I also recommend Diaro (Play Store), which is similar in functionality, cross platform (Web, Android, iOS), and has a little more organization tools (folders in addition to tags). I prefer Journey because it has a cleaner interface and more views to play with, but if you don't like to use Chrome or switch between iOS/Android then it might be better for you.
